articles.title: Nations Championship: England will not get carried away by win against All Blacks - Matt Dawson
articles.summary: In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the final round of Nations Championship fixtures.
articles.body:
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the final round of Nations Championship fixtures.

If England had produced that performance two years ago against New Zealand, there would have been a lap of honour and wild celebrations.

Saturday felt like business. Job done, move on. And that is how it should be.

It was a record victory for a northern hemisphere side against the All Blacks, yet at full-time you would hardly have known it.

Even the post-match messaging from their leaders - Maro Itoje, Ellis Genge and Steve Borthwick - was that this performance had always been in them and that nobody was surprised.

A tired but hurting New Zealand side will arrive at Allianz Stadium next Saturday looking for revenge.

England beat the All Blacks in back-to-back Tests in 2002 and 2003. Matching that achievement on Saturday was a significant statement.

Three consecutive wins over New Zealand, followed by a third-place finish, would leave England in a strong position heading into 2027, when the Rugby World Cup takes place in Australia.

Lose, though, and it will be a waste of some great momentum.

We have had many a false dawn with Borthwick's England, but something feels different this time.

For me, that comes down to the players taking responsibility.

Many of us ex-pros called for it during the Six Nations, and finally we are seeing the players take the lead on the style of rugby they want to play.

It is an exciting, free-flowing brand of attacking rugby that mirrors what they are used to playing in the Prem.

England's backs can compete with the very best and they tore through New Zealand on multiple occasions.

Credit also has to go to Borthwick for allowing the players to take control. That, in itself, shows how he is learning and evolving as a head coach.

Once players start getting 40, 50, 60 or 70 caps, they know more about certain aspects of the game than the coach because they are the ones out there experiencing it.

If the environment does not allow players to turn around and say 'this isn't going to work', then it is never going to work.

The reports before the Australia game suggested honest conversations took place, with the players wanting a greater say in how the team operates.

The Six Nations was probably a big turning point. The change in mood and the feel-good factor are clear in the way England are carrying themselves.

They now feel in control and, crucially, have a genuine sense of ownership in shaping the team and how it plays.

'An enormous statement about English rugby'

Lewis Moody, a former team-mate of mine, joining the team to face the New Zealand haka was an enormous statement about English rugby.

Whether you are playing in 2026 or 1926, this is England rugby. We are together.

It was a united and extraordinary moment, one that will stay with me until the day I die. There was a clear bond as Lewis embraced every England player before leaving the pitch.

That was a huge driver for England. They were able to show their emotional vulnerability before quickly switching into game mode.

A record victory over New Zealand was so fitting for the occasion, but I am not getting overly carried away by the big scoreline.

The southern hemisphere teams are coming towards the end of a brutally long season. They have done a lot of travelling and played considerably more international rugby.

New Zealand and South Africa, in particular, had the added emotion of four summer Tests against each other in the 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series.

The Springboks also looked tired and strangely out of sorts in their defeat by Ireland.

At the beginning of the tournament, we were probably looking at it thinking it was a shame that the two top teams in the world were going to be on the same side of the draw.

Now, they have both lost back-to-back games, with injuries also playing a part.

England should not get carried away, by any stretch. It will be incredibly difficult for New Zealand to pick themselves up after that defeat.

The flight is waiting to take them home, they need some rest and will want to start thinking about next year's World Cup.

England, by contrast, will be chomping at the bit. They have momentum, and everybody is itching to get the white shirt on and run out at Allianz Stadium.

Saturday will provide another really good test of how England deal with being favourites. I expect changes to be made, but I still expect England to win.

After some difficult moments during this World Cup cycle, we are now seeing proper depth start to come through.

I can name at least two quality options in every position.

Can win over All Blacks finally break England's boom-bust cycle?

Rugby Union Weekly: England eclipse the All Blacks after record-breaking win

Ex-captain Moody joins England in emotional haka response

France will probably go into the final as favourites against South Africa.

Closing out back-to-back Six Nations titles and last week's victory over the world champions has given them the confidence to believe they can secure further silverware.

The Nations Championship has been a big success in replicating tournament rugby and, crucially, teaching teams how to win tight games.

Never write off the Springboks, but France are flying high after their performances against Argentina and South Africa.

Rassie Erasmus' side have lost back-to-back games, ending any perceived sense of invincibility. However, they only needed a point to reach the final and got that in Dublin.

Now it is winner takes all, and the world champions - with back-to-back Rugby World Cups and Rugby Championships behind them - should be in their element.

Fabien Galthie has rotated his squad tremendously well, and France will have more energy heading into next Sunday's final.

Those two points gained away to New Zealand with a second-string team in July ultimately proved decisive in the final standings.

I would have loved England to be competing for a trophy on this final weekend, but France have been the more consistent side.

The tables have turned, and suddenly the top teams in the world are in the northern hemisphere.

That is the magic of this new tournament. Everything can change in the space of a week.

Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Alastair Telfer.

articles.title: Wales show signs of progress despite defeat by Australia, say Scrum V pundits
articles.summary: Wales believe they are on the up despite failing to back up their win against New Zealand when beaten by Australia in the Nations Championship.
articles.body:
For experienced hooker Ryan Elias, the proof of Wales' progress came when he looked around in the post-match huddle and saw heads down after a narrow defeat by Australia.

Steve Tandy's side failed to back up their historic victory against New Zealand when edged out 29-26 by the Wallabies in the Nations Championship.

Wales could not claim another scalp against the Aussies, who are two places above them in seventh in World Rugby's rankings, but they went close.

"It wasn't that long ago, not even 12 months ago, that we probably would have been chuffed with that result," said 54-cap forward Elias.

"You look around the circle at the end of that game and there were boys with heads down because this is one that got away.

"That just shows the growth of the group and the belief that's coming."

Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat

Wales should have picked Botham, says flanker's dad

Next Sunday is the one-year anniversary of Wales' 73-0 defeat by South Africa in Cardiff, a hammering that was followed by heavy Six Nations losses against England and France.

Tandy's squad have since enjoyed victories against Italy, Fiji and Japan before the statement success against New Zealand.

"It's hard to recreate what they did against the All Blacks," former Wales centre Tom Shanklin said on Scrum V podcast.

"It's hard to get to that level every week, but it was really positive. We're still in a building phase.

"We said the best thing about the Japan game was that it was a bonus-point win, and that was about it.

"That feels a long time ago. We've come a long, long way.

"The effort was there against Australia, but there just wasn't that clinical edge and maybe that's a psychological thing."

Wales were nervy 28-21 winners at the start of November against a Japan side who have since been thumped by England and Scotland.

They face the Brave Blossoms again on Saturday (13:10 GMT) at Nations Championship finals weekend at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

"This is a big game now to see how much we've changed and developed from the first game of the campaign to the last," said Shanklin.

Wales chalked up four-try bonuses in all three games in Cardiff and have added to their threat from driving line-out.

They have profited from consistency at 10-12-13 with Sam Costelow, Max Llewellyn and Eddie James.

"You're seeing a team that seems to have found an attack," said Shanklin.

"Matt Sherratt has worked really hard with them and we've got various options now, we're not too predictable.

"We're playing with a lot more quick ball and we're quite clever in how we're breaking teams down.

"There are multiple options now when taking the ball to the line and we are getting it into the hands of our strike runners."

Wales did, however, waste a number of 22 entries in the first half and the final try by Ryan Elias came after pressure that ate into the clock.

"We were really good up to about five or 10 metres out, then we lost the detail," said former Wales and Lions wing Alex Cuthbert on Scrum V.

"We didn't do a lot to get held up over the line. We were quite predictable around the corner and Australia won every physical battle and were very good defensively."

Louis Rees-Zammit vowed in the summer that he would fire during his second season back in rugby after his crack at the NFL.

The 6ft 2in wing has been true to his word and arguably the 2021 Lions tourist is a better player now than he was before heading to America in 2024.

Rees-Zammit provided more evidence of his pace and added power when creating Blair Murray's try down the right in the second half.

"I was in line with where Zam had the ball and thought that surely Harry Potter was not going to give him the outside," said Cuthbert.

"It was only three or four yards and he did a shimmy in and if he gets half a yard outside then he is so quick.

"But now he is so strong from the hip down, so broke through Potter and then [Joseph-Aukuso] Suaalii tried to come across and it looked like they got an arm on him.

"It's just that power and watch Rees-Zammit carry now and he makes yard after contact."

The Bristol back has returned to wing and Murray, one of Wales' star performers in 2024-25, has profited from starting at full-back.

"He's a class player isn't he?" said the Scarlets man about Rees-Zammit. "He is one of the best wingers in the world, and he shows it week in and week out.

"We're working well together, you know. Whether I'm putting him through holes or he's getting through and passing it back inside.

"That connection is growing and we want to get the ball in our hands as much as we can."

The pair and experienced wing Josh Adams look sure to start the Six Nations, fitness permitting.

Tandy opted to change a winning team, going back to the starters that faced Japan.

His decision to rest flanker James Botham is in the spotlight after his man-of-the-match display against the All Blacks.

Alex Mann was to the fore in a different way despite suffering a painful early poke in the eye from team-mate Ben Carter, coming up with a turnover, claiming five line-outs and riling the Wallabies.

"You're certainly looking at the squad now thinking you're a lot more confident if there are injuries," said Shanklin.

"To have strength and depth with two quality players in every single position then you have got to play them.

"You cannot just have your first team out every game, then when players come in they are not going to be up to that level or have that experience. You've got to mix and match a bit."

Tandy is poised to rotate his squad for Saturday's fixture against Japan, when Wales travel to London after three games on home soil.

It will be the first game of a double-header on the day, and a warm-up for England's rematch with New Zealand.

Wales' win against the All Blacks gave a boost to ticket sales for the Wallabies fixture despite the late kick-off time.

The crowd of 66,307 was larger than the 52,425 against Japan and 55,152 against New Zealand.

Crucially, after the lows of last season's heavy defeats by South Africa and France, the connection seems strong between Tandy's team and the supporters.

"The atmosphere was amazing again," said Cuthbert, who scored two tries in the bedlam of the famous 2013 victory against England.

"You've got to give credit to the Principality Stadium staff, they are really making the place have that bit of theatre and entertainment."

Wales will hope it gives them an extra lift for the visits of Ireland and England in the Six Nations.

articles.title: Wales v Japan: Steve Tandy set for Nations Championship play-off changes
articles.summary: The choices facing Steve Tandy as the Wales head coach gets set to rotate his side for the Nations Championship finale against Japan.
articles.body:
Wales head coach Steve Tandy, with one eye on the World Cup, vowed to rotate his side for Nations Championship finals weekend even before his side had faced Australia.

Hopes of an autumn clean sweep - something only achieved once in 2018 under Warren Gatland - were dashed by the Wallabies at the Principality Stadium on Saturday.

Wales dust themselves down before finishing the November campaign against familiar foes Japan on Saturday (13:10 GMT).

The Six Nations is not a time for experimenting, so it presents a rare chance to have a look at players in the countdown to next year's World Cup in Australia.

Wales spluttered to victory against Eddie Jones' side at the start of the month and will expect a more comfortable success at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

The fixture, a fifth meeting with the Brave Blossoms in 16 months, presents a chance for Tandy to test his squad depth.

Did beaten Wales still show they have come a long way?

Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat

Eleven of Wales' players started against Japan, New Zealand and Australia - Blair Murray, Louis Rees-Zammit, Eddie James, Max Llewellyn, Sam Costelow, Tomos Williams, Nicky Smith, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Dafydd Jenkins and Jac Morgan.

It is fair to assume that plenty of big hitters will watch from the stands at Twickenham, after the mental and physical demands of the past fortnight.

"I can rotate the team and we'll still put in a performance. It doesn't matter who wears the shirt, we've got to perform," said Tandy.

"Whenever we put a team out, the objective is to win a Test match. That will be no different next Saturday."

The core of the first-choice team will remain in England after the Japan game and rejoin their clubs in the Prem.

Former Wales and Lions wing Alex Cuthbert urged Tandy to resist the temptation to give the frontline players a breather.

"We need to put our best team out. We really want to put a marker down against Japan," he said on the Scrum V podcast.

"It's an opportunity to really put Japan to the sword if we really want to take some momentum into the Six Nations."

The Japanese are stretched by injury and conceded 24 tries in defeats by England and Scotland.

Wales fielded the same starting line-up against Japan and Australia either side of the New Zealand victory.

Man of the match against the All Blacks James Botham went from the XV to missing out completely against the Wallabies, much to the frustration of his father Liam.

Botham's fellow Cardiff back-row forward Taine Basham and Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb suffered the same fate.

Versatile forward Taine Plumtree has proved his worth from the bench in the past two fixtures but might hope for a first Test start since Scotland in the third round of the 2026 Six Nations.

Tandy is spoilt for choice in the back-row and gave promising Exeter flanker Kane James a second cap off the bench against the Wallabies.

Wales have also developed depth at loose-head prop to the extent that strong-running Rhys Carre, Welsh Rugby Writers' Association (WRWA) player of the year after his Six Nations exploits, missed out against New Zealand and Australia.

Smith has started all three November Tests and Ospreys' Gareth Thomas has been strong off the bench.

Wales selected three uncapped players in their initial Nations Championship squad with Cardiff loose-head prop Rhys Barratt, who played against the Barbarians in the summer, joined by the Dragons pair of scrum-half Che Hope and centre Aneurin Owen.

That figure became four when in-form Scarlets wing Macs Page got a call-up due to Rio Dyer's hamstring injury.

Tandy has given first caps to nine players since taking the reins in the summer of 2025 and could hit double figures at Twickenham.

There are seven other players in the squad who are yet to feature this month.

Centre Joe Hawkins failed to get off the bench against the Wallabies, when he was also Costelow's cover at fly-half.

Hooker Liam Belcher, tight-head Keiron Assiratti, lock Seb Davies, wing Ellis Mee and wing or full-back Tom Rogers have had no minutes, while fly-half Jarrod Evans was called into the squad last week when Dan Edwards suffered an injury in training.

Reuben Morgan-Williams scored a sniping try in the win against the Barbarians in June.

The Ospreys scrum-half will hope to wear nine on his back for the first time in a Test match on the return to Twickenham.

Wales have been reliant on world-class Tomos Williams, and his deputy Kieran Hardy faces a fitness race for the World Cup after a serious knee injury.

Morgan-Williams was called into the fray for the last quarter of an hour against New Zealand and was introduced just five minutes into the second half against the Wallabies.

"Reuben played a fair part of the game and did really well," said Tandy. "He was very accurate in what he did.

"Tomos had a tight groin and we will assess that, but we've got to find out about Reuben."

Wales are scheduled to name their team on Thursday morning.

articles.title: Ireland 20-17 South Africa: Andy Farrell says Springboks win 'sets us up nicely'
articles.summary: Ireland head coach Andy Farrell says his side's victory over South Africa "sets us up nicely" for the the countdown to next year's World Cup.
articles.body:
After Ireland's win over world champions South Africa on Saturday, Andy Farrell had one eye on the past, and another on what is to come.

It was a result that had left Ireland's head coach brimming with pride, as they ended a run of six straight defeats against either the Springboks, New Zealand or France.

With the World Cup now just 10 months away, it is all part of the bigger picture as Ireland aim to progress past the quarter-finals for the first time, with the ultimate goal of lifting the Webb Ellis Cup.

"Whether we lose by three or win by three, you understand how you apply yourself in a big game like that, and it doesn't get any bigger," Farrell said after the 20-17 win.

"You're always trying to kick on to the next level, and sometimes you don't know what that level is because you've never been there as a group.

"But this group is like that. We're trying to do new things together, and it sets us up nicely to keep kicking on."

Farrell looked back to the opening three matches of the Nations Championship in July, when he handed a number of players minutes at international level against Australia and Japan - such as Nick Timoney, Tom Stewart and Tom Clarkson.

Those players played a key role in downing the Springboks in Dublin as second-half replacements.

"We chose to take players to the Southern Hemisphere who had not had that type of experience.

"It's never going to be smelling of roses in that regard [performances over 80 minutes], so you end up where you're at, but we grew as a group, so therefore it's priceless for us."

Did Springboks win change the narrative for Ireland?

Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable

Ireland beat the Boks: Post-match reaction with Josh Van der Flier and Mike McCarthy

Given how the tables were weighted, Ireland would have topped the southern hemisphere table by two points.

But the northern hemisphere's domination of the inaugural competition meant a more condensed table, and a fifth-place play-off against Australia will be their reward.

But Friday will be another tough test against a Wallabies side who were one missed penalty away from beating Ireland in Sydney in July.

Speaking before he knew who Ireland would be playing, and when, Farrell denied that playing for fifth place would be an anti-climax.

"You can only deal with what's in front of you," he said.

"We've got another week of international rugby together. We're in the green shirt, and that's special and it's a privilege, so we'll look forward to that."

Ireland's team selection to face South Africa had a surprise as captain Dan Sheehan, who usually plays at hooker, was named to start at number eight.

It was only his second professional start in the back row, with his first outing coming for Leinster against Munster before the international window.

Farrell's decision was certainly justified as Sheehan more than played his role in a scrum that held its own against the world-leading Springbok pack.

"He's so calm, isn't he? I spoke to him over the last couple of weeks about all sorts of things, about number eight, but he wasn't worried and it doesn't bother him in the slightest," said Farrell.

"It's like, 'why are you asking me that question?'. It's almost like an insult. He's so calm, he's such a gifted rugby player.

"That's his character. He just sees it for what it is and he gets on with it. That calm and influence has a knock-on effect that goes through the team."

Another standout for Ireland was Jamison Gibson-Park, whose experience and guile helped the hosts get over the line as the Boks piled on late pressure.

One clearing kick, from his own try line to the halfway line, was a particular standout in a game filled with classy moments.

Farrell described the 34-year-old's kicking as "immense", and said he is getting better with each passing year.

"He got us out of trouble so many times. You almost expect it from him, but you shouldn't," said Farrell.

"He is growing the whole time. I've never seen him in this good of nick, it just shows the hunger that he's got.

"That's what we've got within our group as well, we've got senior players who are constantly working so hard to continue to get better."

articles.title: Nations Championship: Rassie Erasmus set to host France watch-along as South Africa coaches deny contact during Ireland loss
articles.summary: South Africa coaches have denied contact with suspended head coach Rassie Erasmus during their 20-17 Nations Championship defeat to Ireland in Dublin; Erasmus streamed a live watch-along in which he could have breached team rules by communicating with staff or criticising officials
articles.body:
Erasmus was barred from having any involvement in matchday activity as part of a six-game ban from World Rugby for questioning whether "match-fixing" and "manipulation" was occurring in rugby after his side's thrilling defeat to France in Paris .

The 54-year-old nevertheless hosted the watch-along from the team's hotel, where he was muted for large spells of the event but could be seen speaking to an unknown party while wearing earbuds and covering his mouth.

The head coach has now announced that he will host another watch-along for South Africa's Nations Championship final clash against France at Twickenham on Sunday, two weeks after he received his ban for his comments on the officiating against the same opposition.

Asked if Erasmus was passing on messages during the Ireland game, Springboks assistant coach Felix Jones said: "I've no idea, we were busy with a Test match."

Fellow assistant coach Mzwandile Stick added: "Maybe he was communicating with his followers on that party that he was having, but with us we were just in the game."

Build-up to the heavyweight contest at the Aviva Stadium was dominated by Erasmus' sanction, with the watch-along representing a potential breach of World Rugby's rules should Erasmus have been recorded criticising any decisions or communicating with any members of the playing or coaching staff.

Jones continued by saying the situation was not a distraction as the Springboks slipped to a second successive loss, before questions on Erasmus were quickly shut down by the team's media officer.

"Thank you for everything this week. The messages, the photos and the support mean a great deal to me," Erasmus said in a post on X on Monday.

"Losing is never nice, but we are still number one in the world and we are in the final of the Nations Cup. So let's go again.

"I'd love to watch it with you. Put the final on your own TV on Sunday and join me."

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell savoured a "big night for everyone who's Irish" and a major stepping stone in his side's journey towards next year's World Cup.

Robert Baloucoune claimed two first-half tries and Ronan Kelleher added another, with a long-range penalty from Sam Prendergast ultimately proving decisive amid a colossal defensive effort.

"It's something that we've been looking forward to and tried to challenge ourselves with about delivering when it matters against top-line sides," said Farrell.

"We knew that this fixture was coming, playing against the world's best - world's best by a stretch at this moment in time, I would have thought so.

"It was a game that we wanted to challenge ourselves and see how we went and obviously fronting up and showing the character that we did and coming out the right side of the win is a big night for everyone who's Irish."

South Africa ensured a pulsating encounter remained tantalisingly poised until the final whistle thanks to scores from Morne van den Berg and Malcolm Marx, plus seven points from the boot of Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu.

"I think we've taken a step forward and that was the aim," said Farrell.

"This game mattered to us in how we prepped for it. We didn't shy away from that and we took it on for what it was, which was a top of the tree game.

"We were able to perform. It wasn't perfect but we managed to come out with a win. The World Cup, it's all about stepping stones and this is a big one that's for sure."

Despite their defeat, South Africa progressed to the Nations Championship final at Twickenham after picking up a losing bonus point, with Ireland contesting the third-place final against Australia.

Asked about Erasmus, Farrell said: "Rassie is his own man and he's a smart guy. He does things for a reason.

"There's always going to be a plan or whatever. I don't know the ins and outs of it.

"The South African boys are in our dressing room having a beer and it's an unspoken rule that you just leave it alone, I would have thought. It is what it is."

articles.title: Lewis Moody says he 'felt ready to play' after former captain joined England to face New Zealand's Haka
articles.summary: Former England captain Lewis Moody joined England to receive the Haka ahead of their 37-12 victory over the All Blacks on Saturday; Moody fronted England's arrow-head formation for the pre-match tradition
articles.body:
Emotional scenes unfolded at Allianz Stadium, as Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) in 2025, walked arm-in-arm with Itoje onto the field.

New Zealand's players clapped as the former England captain took up position at the front of England's arrow-head formation - between Itoje and Ellis Genge - to accept the challenge of the Haka.

Moody, who won 71 international caps during his career, had presented England's players with their matchday shirts at their Pennyhill Park base on Friday, and revealed Ollie Chessum had jokingly urged him to stay on the pitch and chase down the first kick.

"I honestly felt ready to play," Moody told BBC Breakfast .

"When the lads were hugging me after the Haka, I was like: 'Right, I'm ready to go'."

"The night before, Ollie Chessum told me where they were going for the first kick-off.

"He was like: 'Mate, if you're up for it, you can chase it!'

"I was almost ready to take him up on that."

In support of Moody's Front Up to Motor Neurone Disease campaign, England's players wore boots as well as special warm-up and arrival kit with the campaign's logo printed on them.

The players also signed warm-up tops and match shirts, which were donated to the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, a charity founded by the late Scotland international Doddie Weir that provides funds for MND research.

"I was really aware that this was something that I would never get to feel again and hadn't felt for over 15 years," Moody said.

"So, I wanted to try and fully take in the moment.

"When I got out there, Maro [Itoje] brought me out there and positioned me.

"Ellis [Genge] embraced me, the bundle of physical energy that he is. That's inspiring in itself, to feel the power that's emanating through his body.

"The noise was almost overwhelming. And then [I tried] to recentre myself and focus on the Haka, through the peripheral vision of the England team that fanned out in front of me.

"It just brought a huge smile, and brought back a lot of wonderful memories of playing with all my former team-mates."

He added: "It was really unique and I feel humbled to have been a part of it."

Front Up to MND are organising a series of coastal walk fundraisers on June 12 2027 to raise money for the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation.

"To have the response that it did and to have the support that it has is only good for the cause that I was there for, which is the Front Up campaign supporting My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, to raise as much money as possible, to have a serious impact on this disease," Moody said.

"We need more drugs that have a significant impact for patients. They are the breakthroughs that we're looking for and this campaign will get us near, if not over the line with that.

"But we need thousands, if not tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of people to support and get involved.

"And hopefully, if you're a little bit inspired or if you just loved watching the game at the weekend, and everything that represented, and you fancied taking on a challenge, come and join us on June 12, walking the coast."

Atkinson: It was special to be a part of

Asked whether Moody's presence motivated England, Seb Atkinson told Sky Sports News:

"Definitely, he came into the hotel last night and gave us some reflections on his career and some reflections on his diagnosis.

"It was really special to be a part of that. I think the lads really took it on board.

"Then to hear the noise of him coming out and taking part in our response to the Haka was really special.

"Also to see his family and his sons and speak to himself [Moody] in the changing rooms after, it just topped it off."

articles.title: Ellie Kildunne: Bristol star responds to Harlequins time-keeping reports
articles.summary: England and Bristol Bears full-back Ellie Kildunne makes a pointed reference to reports that poor time-keeping was behind her Harlequins exit.
articles.body:
England and Bristol Bears full-back Ellie Kildunne marked her return to former club Harlequins with two tries, victory and a pointed reference to reports that her poor time-keeping was behind her Stoop exit.

Kildunne, with a watch drawn on taping around her wrist, ran in two first-half tries in a 48-21 victory at the Stoop in the first round of the PWR on Sunday.

"You've all seen the headlines. Why would I have a watch on my wrist?" the 27-year-old told TNT Sport after the match.

She later posted a photo of the watch drawing on Instagram , external with the caption: "Right on time."

Kildunne, who was not quoted in Quins' announcement of her departure in June, subsequently said she was "gutted" to be leaving and that it was "as much a shock to me as everyone else".

The Bears, who also signed Wales back row Bethan Lewis in the summer, finished eighth in the nine-team top flight last season.

Kildunne was not the only England star to enjoy success against the former club, with Tatyana Heard, who was part of big-spending Sale's summer recruitment drive, enjoying a 31-17 win over Gloucester-Hartpury.

Gloucester-Hartpury, who won the title three times in a row between 2023 and 2025, are without a head coach after Dan Murphy left on the eve of the season.

Champions Saracens and Ealing Trailfinders, who lost to Saracens in June's final, best Leicester and Loughborough Lightning respectively.

articles.title: Rugby gran MJ eyes Christmas number one with techno track
articles.summary: MJ, aged 70, is releasing her debut single to "dance and rave to" at Christmas, on Friday.
articles.body:
A 70-year-old gran is set to release her very own high-energy Christmas charity single vying to be this year's number one.

MJ, from Rugby, says her festive techno track Christmas Day Is Coming is one to "dance and rave to rather than the melody ones" and is "something different".

"I just thought to myself, 'I think we need a change', and I just started writing about Christmas and enjoying ourselves," said MJ, who records as Christmas Gran.

The £1 track is released on Friday and each sale will boost national charity Crisis that helps people experiencing homelessness.

MJ said that while the song is upbeat and a track to move to, she wants people to think about those who are "lonely, lost, and on the streets in the cold throughout the winter".

"If we can raise as much money as we, can it will help them through the coldest and darkest days of their life," she said.

"I've seen them taking food out of the bins that people have half eaten and it's just wrong.

"You wouldn't even let a dog lie on the streets on its own and they're fallen people for whatever reason; they could have lost their job or not been able to pay the mortgage or the rent."

MJ said she had "really enjoyed" creating the track and she "felt amazing" when she heard it.

Andy Kulesza, the track's producer whose best friend happens to be MJ's sister, said the single was "great".

Kulesza is is also a musician himself, having had some success as part of electronic trio A Million Sons, from Nottingham.

"I love it and hopefully the listeners will like it as well," he told BBC CWR.

"Seeing a 70-year-old great granny singing a banging techno cheesy dance song for Christmas, I thought nobody's really done that yet.

"I think nowadays with music you need something that's going to stand out and shock people, and this does that."

Kulesza said MJ has suffered significant loss in her life, but has stayed positive, funny and giving.

Turning to her future in the music industry, MJ has set her sights on doing a rap song.

"I would like to do a rap song with somebody so Stormzy if you are listening," she said. "He needs to get in touch because I've got another one coming out."

articles.title: Dave Rennie backed by New Zealand Rugby after two defeats in a row
articles.summary: All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie has received the unequivocal backing of his bosses at New Zealand Rugby.
articles.body:
All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie has received the unequivocal backing of his bosses at New Zealand Rugby to lead the team through to next year's World Cup.

Rennie's side have suffered back-to-back defeats in the November leg of the Nations Championship and have lost five times in the calendar year for the first time since 1998.

"We have complete confidence in Rens," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said.

"His position is not in question. He will take the team to the World Cup. That is not going to change."

Rennie was appointed in March and started his All Blacks tenure in style, dispatching France and Ireland in the July part of the Nations Championship before a memorable victory over world champions South Africa in the Springboks' spiritual home of Ellis Park.

But New Zealand lost the next three Tests against the Boks to fall 3-1 in the 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' [RGR] series, and, although two convincing wins over Australia retained the Bledisloe Cup, the All Blacks have endured a difficult tour of Europe.

A first loss to Wales in 73 years was followed by an English rout in Twickenham, while the All Blacks have also been hit by the tragic death of their long-serving head of security Logan Cadwallader.

The emotional toll of Cadwallader's passing along with the arduous schedule this year are thought to be two mitigating factors behind the dip in form, and New Zealand's administrators will review the impact of the RGR series when planning its return in 2030.

Lancaster added that the union will look to make a call in the middle of next year as to whether Rennie takes charge of the team beyond the 2027 World Cup.

"We will conduct a full campaign and season review following this year, as we always do," he said.

"That will inform how we approach next year, but it will also inform our discussions around what the contract situation looks like beyond next year.

"Our intention is to make all those decisions and have clarity before we go into the World Cup. Nothing has changed from when we appointed Rens earlier this year.

"He is a world-class coach. We went through the most rigorous appointment process that I have been involved in, which included spending time observing him coaching in Japan with his team and in his environment."

articles.title: Tommy Freeman and Fin Smith included in England squad for New Zealand rematch in final Nations Championship clash

Elsewhere, head coach Steve Borthwick has added Saracens' Noah Caluori to the squad, with the winger potentially in line to make his third Test appearance for England.

England will hope for a repeat performance to seal third place in the inaugural Nations Championship, having proved far too strong for New Zealand at the weekend. The match takes place a day before France play South Africa at Twickenham in the final.

England's dominant win last time out has impacted the global rankings, with Borthwick's side climbing from fifth to fourth and the All Blacks plummeting from second to fifth.

articles.title: Tommy Freeman: England wing in contention for All Blacks rematch
articles.summary: England wing Tommy Freeman is in contention for Saturday's Nations Championship play-off meeting with New Zealand.
articles.body:
England wing Tommy Freeman is in contention for Saturday's Nations Championship play-off meeting with New Zealand.

The 25-year-old has been a key part of England's backline this year, starting nine Tests in a row for before being rotated out of the side for their comprehensive win over Japan on 14 November.

He was due to return for the 37-12 win over the All Blacks on Saturday, but a thigh issue forced his withdrawal in the hours before kick-off.

Harlequins' Cadan Murley was called into the side to replace Freeman and impressed in an emphatic England performance.

Head coach Steve Borthwick has bolstered his back-three options, which also include Gloucester's Will Joseph, by calling up Saracens' 20-year-old Noah Caluori.

Caluori, who finished as joint-top try scorer in last year's Prem alongside Freeman, crossed on his England debut against Fiji in July and was a late replacement in the win over Argentina a week later.

He also scored two tries in a England A's win over an Argentine equivalent earlier this month.

Fly-half Fin Smith, who came off 55 minutes into the win over the All Blacks with cramp, is also in a 37-strong squad who have gathered at England's training base to prepare for Saturday's third-place play-off.

England finished a point short of France in the northern hemisphere standings of the new format, missing out on a place in Sunday's Nations Championship final against South Africa.

The result of England and New Zealand's meeting, along with the weekend's other five matches at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium, will contribute to a Ryder Cup-style points race for the inaugural hemisphere shield.

articles.title: Prem Rugby: Worcester Warriors and Coventry show interest but on right terms
articles.summary: Champ clubs Coventry and Warriors confirm interest in Prem places  - but not if it puts their clubs at financial risk.
articles.body:
Midlands clubs Coventry and Worcester Warriors have both confirmed their interest in taking up the potential offer of a place in the Prem - but not if it puts their clubs at any sort of financial risk.

Prem Rugby last week opened a registration process for teams to apply for the 2029-30 season, with the aim of expanding the league back up from the current 10 clubs to 12.

The lack of depth in English top-flight club rugby has been a concern ever since London Irish followed Worcester and Wasps in folding at the end of the 2022-23 season.

Wasps, originally a London club who played at Sudbury before moving to football club Queens Park Rangers' Loftus Road home and then on to Adams Park, Wycombe, were based in Coventry, at the CBS Arena, when they went out of business.

They announced in 2024 that they intended to return to the south east and were looking for a new home in Kent - and last week were reported to have put in a planning application for a new community training ground at Swanley.

Worcester are into their second season in the rebranded Champ following their reformation, while Coventry, one of the powerhouses of English rugby union in the days before the sport went fully professional in 1996, have not played in the top flight since the first season of the Courage League in 1987-88, when they were relegated.

"The Prem are right in trying to expand," Cov executive chairman Jon Sharp told BBC Sport.

"It's very hard for their clubs only having nine home games each.

"And we would love to go to the Prem. We owe it to our history. We owe it to our supporters. And I'm prepared to spend money sensibly on the extension of our facilities.

"I'm happy to spend some millions to do that, but to spend £20m to buy a P-share (the ownership stake held by each Prem member club)? No. I've made it clear that I'm not doing that."

Prem opens registration for expansion to 12 teams

Worcester have to maintain standards - Everard

Top of the list of the Prem's requirements for any team is a minimum stadium capacity of 10,001. Cov's Butts Park Arena, since their old, traditional 10,000-capacity Coundon Road was torn down in 2004 for housing redevelopment, is only 5,250.

"The right thing for the Prem to do is relax the minimum operating standards they introduced and do away with the need for a P-share," added Sharp. "Or at least make it a lot easier to acquire one and restore promotion and relegation.

"They started the process back when they were reduced to 10 clubs by the collapse of Wasps, Worcester and London Irish and then started approaching clubs individually.

"They approached Cov because of our history, and because our stadium is not far off. But we'd still need about £25m to meet that minimum capacity of 10,000."

On the weekend when Coventry and Worcester met at the Butts Park Arena, the hosts went level on points with their opponents in the Champ thanks to a 57-42 win in a thrilling game of 14 tries.

But, while Warriors conceded over 50 points on the ground for the second year running, the two clubs are at least on the same side as regards their demands.

"Yes, we're interested," Warriors chief executive Stephen Vaughan told BBC Hereford & Worcester. "Yes, we will be kicking the tyres on the request for information.

"We aspire to play in the highest possible place that we can, but we will not jeopardise the future of the club.

"I can give every Warriors fan out there every reassurance that we will investigate every possible route to it.

"We are very, very sought after within the Prem. But, at the moment, and we've been very clear on this, the financial situation is so penal that we would jeopardise the very future of the club if we were to go up on the current criteria."

articles.title: Women's smaller ball trial extended after positive Sevens results
articles.summary: World Rugby extends the women's 4.5 ball trial for a second season after releasing data showing improvements in several areas of the game and receiving "overwhelmingly positive" feedback from players and coaches.
articles.body:
World Rugby has extended the women's 4.5 ball trial for a second season after releasing data showing improvements in several areas of the game and receiving "overwhelmingly positive" feedback from players and coaches.

Data collected from the Sevens trials showed ruck speeds were on average 10% faster, while a four-year trend of declining passing rates was reversed. Goal kicking accuracy was unaffected.

The 4.5 size ball will be used in the 2026-27 HSBC SVNS Series and Championship, starting on 28 November in Dubai.

World Rugby confirmed that a decision on the 4.5 ball for the whole of the women's game would be taken in February, with data from the XVs game still being gathered.

The smaller ball debate has split opinion, with many England players expressing their dislike of the trial, including fly-half Zoe Harrison describing it as the "worst decision ever" earlier this year.

However, Wales wing Lisa Neumann is a fan, saying "it's changed the game" for her passing because of improved grip on the ball.

The data gathered in Sevens compares four seasons of size 5 ball data with one season using the 4.5 ball.

The home nations played with the 4.5 ball in the recent WXV tournament but those who have returned to Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR) are back playing with a size 5.

World Rugby confirmed that PWR declined the opportunity to use the smaller ball this season, while New Zealand's Super Rugby Aupiki and Australia's Super W opted to use the 4.5.

World Rugby's Chief Player Welfare and Rugby Sevens Officer Mark Harrington confirmed that the timing of the trial is specific.

"This was the window of the 12 to 18 month period where it didn't necessarily conflict with Olympic qualification or Rugby World Cup qualification," he said.

"Wherever we land [in February], it's the same ball for both codes."

Should World Rugby decide to adopt the 4.5 ball, Head of Women's Game Sally Horrox said: "There'll need to be some proper planning and a sensible transition.

"You don't want to put that burden on the game or that opportunity on the game without having the chance to plan."

She also confirmed that support for the community game would be taken into consideration if changes were implemented.

"We are considering the economics of the situation and any phase change or rollout," she added.

"If a change is recommended, then we, the unions and the high-performance committee would weigh up the costs, the supply and the impact on the community game before anything happened. That would be part of the conversation in February."

Additional reporting by Alex Brotherton.

articles.title: O'Toole relishing role on Ireland's 'Tom Squad'
articles.summary: Ireland's Tom O'Toole believes coming on in his side's narrow victory over back-to-back world champions South Africa represents the "ultimate challenge" for...
articles.body:
With Ireland's win over the Springboks on Saturday hanging in the balance until the final whistle, Andy Farrell's bench had to play a considerable part in getting the 20-17 success over the line.

Given South Africa's fearsome scrum, a set-piece in the shadow of their own posts was among the most nervy moments of a frantic endgame.

Up against the visitors' famed 'Bomb Squad', Ireland's replacement front-row of Tom O'Toole, Tom Stewart and Tom Clarkson - now dubbed the 'Tom Squad' - held their own long enough for the ball to find its way to Nick Timoney at the base.

"The Tom Squad's doing well, I thought it was funny" said the 28-year-old of the new nickname.

"Tom Squad, it's official. Tom Squad shoes, Tom Squad t-shirts. We'll maybe start small, but we'll hopefully get a few more opportunities together to build the reputation a little bit, build the brand."

On the late scrum, that saw O'Toole go head-to-head with South African tight-head prop Thomas du Toit with the game on the line, the Ulster player said it was a "surreal moment".

He added: "As soon as I got the nod to go in, to rip in, three points up with 10 minutes to go, I was kind of going, 'right, here we go, this is another development for me on my journey as an individual'.

"I was like, 'well, this is the ultimate challenge'.

"To get a five-metre scrum in front of your own posts with a couple of minutes to go, and Thomas du Toit against you, it's a pretty surreal moment.

"It was probably the hardest scrum that you can get as a front-rower, maybe."

Until last season, O'Toole was predominantly a tight-head prop but switched sides for Ireland during the 2026 Six Nations when injuries robbed Andy Farrell of multiple loose-head options.

Still relatively new to the position, O'Toole believes his 10 previous caps earned on left-side of the scrum helped to settle any nerves against the back-to-back world champions.

"I had a similar scrum in the Six Nations against Italy, pretty much in the same spot, so I maybe just thought about that, reflected that for a split second," he said.

"I was like, 'well, I've been here before, tight game, not long to go, five-metre scrum', and it just gave me that confidence that I'd be able to deliver that again.

"It just brought me back down to keeping calm in my head and executing my role, doing my job."

In between appearances in the Six Nations and Nations Championship southern series as a loose-head, all O'Toole's outings for his province Ulster were back at tight-head.

The presence of Wallaby Angus Bell in Belfast last season was no doubt a big reason for those selections, and O'Toole has solely played loose-head this season.

While Ireland team-mate Andrew Porter is a prominent example of a prop who switched sides not once but twice in their career, O'Toole is planning to stick at loose-head.

"I'm loving loose-head. I've obviously got a fair few opportunities off it within the last few months," he said.

"It's been a class development. I think for me, where I am in my career at this stage, it's been a class challenge, but I think first and foremost for the moment definitely loose-head.

"I knew I had the capabilities of doing it. Then I think the more experience I got, the more confidence, and then the more I just started to kind of go 'right, ok'. I think I have a much deeper and better understanding of it."

articles.title: Louis Rees-Zammit: Wales wing hitting new levels as 2.0 version
articles.summary: Wales wing Louis Rees-Zammit may not have made the cut in American football, but his gridiron crucible has seen him reformed as an improved version on his rugby union return.
articles.body:
Australia wing Harry Potter had Louis Rees-Zammit exactly where he wanted him.

As Wales attacked in Cardiff on Saturday, Potter showed Rees-Zammit the outside – a four-metre channel between him and the touchline.

The touchline is a defender's best friend. An extra defender. The edge of the cliff. It would take something extraordinary to beat Potter without running out of ground.

A shake of the hips and a change of direction later, Potter was diving like a cricketer in the outfield, grasping at thin air. Rees-Zammit was on his way to setting up a wonderful try for Blair Murray.

Rees-Zammit has been turning heads for years. On the pitch with his pace, off it with his pristine teeth and pop star looks.

But it wasn't raw speed that had left Potter on the turf.

This was Rees-Zammit 2.0 - more than just speed.

Who should Wales pick for autumn finale v Japan?

Did beaten Wales still show they have come a long way?

Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat

Alex Cuthbert knows a thing or two about running. A former national-level 400m runner and British and Irish Lions wing, he spent much of his rugby career working on his technique.

What fascinates him about Rees-Zammit now is not his speed but how he generates it.

"His leg drive and strength from his knee to his hip has got so much stronger," said Cuthbert, who scored 17 tries in 57 Tests for Wales.

The difference is most apparent not over 100 metres but over four or five, changing direction and accelerating before a defender can adjust his feet.

"If you do that shimmy and you stand any sort of player up, you can't recover. Literally can't recover," Cuthbert said.

Cuthbert attributes much of that development to Rees-Zammit's 18 months in American football with the Kansas City Chiefs and Jacksonville Jaguars.

"I thought last season he was a little bit heavy. He looked like a running back last year, whereas this year he is more of a wide receiver," Cuthbert said.

A running back, says Cuthbert, powers through traffic, a wide receiver thrives in open space. He now sees elements of both in Rees-Zammit.

Rees-Zammit's coach at Bristol Bears, Pat Lam, estimates he returned from America eight or nine kilograms heavier.

"What was very clear was his pace was still there, if not quicker, but he was a bigger man and he needed to adjust," said Lam.

Lam is arguably one of rugby's most system-driven coaches. Understanding your role is fundamental at Bristol, where only a select few are afforded the freedom to deviate from the script.

Having established himself as a wing before his American adventure, Rees-Zammit was keen to experiment on his return to rugby.

"He spoke to me about a desire to play full-back and give full-back a go," said Lam.

Lam sees the modern full-back as an auxiliary centre in attack, responsible for creating opportunities for others.

Rees-Zammit's greatest gift is exploiting them.

"But we had to go through that process for him to actually say to me, 'Pat, I'm a world-class winger and I'm a world-class finisher'. And I said, 'I agree'," Lam said.

According to Lam, Rees-Zammit now considers himself a wing who can cover full-back, rather than a full-back who can play on the wing.

Another moment from Saturday offered a reminder of Rees-Zammit's extraordinary pace when Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i intercepted a Welsh pass and set off downfield.

The Australian, a formidable athlete in his own right, had a head start of at least five metres.

One commentator confidently declared he would not be caught.

The speed has always been there. The numbers reveal how much more there is to his game now.

Rees-Zammit scored five tries in 10 Premiership appearances for Bristol last season. This season he has matched that tally in five games, beating 28 defenders and making 12 clean breaks.

Against Japan earlier in November, he beat 13 defenders and made more line breaks in 80 minutes than in the entire Six Nations, when he started all five games at full-back.

But Rees-Zammit is not the only thing that has changed since March, Wales have changed too

Even the quickest wing in the world is of limited use if he receives the ball standing still with two defenders in front of him.

"But as a winger, you do rely on your boys inside you," said Cuthbert.

With Wales generating more momentum up front, Cuthbert highlights Blair Murray's ability to engage defenders before releasing Rees-Zammit.

Wales are also deploying both wings on the same side of the field. Rees-Zammit and Josh Adams combining for full-back Murray's try was a fine example.

Scrum-half Tomos Williams has perfected the art of the sharp, accurate pass that bypasses players and gets the ball into the wider channels early.

It helped create Rees-Zammit's try against New Zealand and, eight minutes into Saturday's game against the Wallabies, looked to have created another.

Having dived for the corner, Rees-Zammit's first instinct on getting to his feet was not to celebrate or appeal to the referee, but to fix his hair.

The try would not survive the television replays. The hair had survived the tackle.

Image matters to Rees-Zammit. He is Welsh rugby's most marketable player, its biggest draw. He puts bums on seats and gets people out of them.

There is a lovely soundtrack to Rees-Zammit receiving the ball in space at the Principality Stadium. A low hum of excitement followed by the rattle of thousands of seats folding up almost simultaneously.

The thrill is in the anticipation, and these days there is rather more to anticipate.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Ireland captain Dan Sheehan to miss Australia Test  after two-game ban for croc-roll
articles.summary: Ireland's stand-in captain Dan Sheehan will be banned for two games after a croc-roll tackle against South Africa and will play no part against Australia on Friday night.
articles.body:
Ireland's stand-in captain Dan Sheehan has been banned for two games after a croc-roll tackle against South Africa and will play no part against Australia on Friday night.

The Leinster forward was shown a yellow card by referee Christophe Ridley in the 72nd minute of Ireland's 20-17 victory over the Springboks in Dublin on Saturday.

That was later upgraded to a red card by the foul play review officer (FPRO) on the basis of World Rugby's Law 9.20d that "a player may remove the jackler from the tackle area by pushing/driving them backwards (including by grabbing the knee/leg), but must not roll, pull or twist an opponent".

The 28-year-old faced a disciplinary hearing on Monday evening where the panel found that the incident was a "low-entry point" offence and merited a two-week ban.

Sheehan will miss Friday's Nations Championship finals weekend fixture against Australia in Twickenham (20:10 GMT) and Leinster's game against Ospreys in the United Rugby Championship (URC) on 4 December.

Sheehan played at number eight against South Africa, the first time he has started at the position in his Test career.

More usually a hooker, his absence requires another change for Ireland at the base of the scrum for what is their final game of 2026.

South Africa win 'sets us up nicely' - Farrell

Did Springboks win change the narrative for Ireland?

Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable

Captain Caelan Doris and two-tour British and Irish Lion Jack Conan have missed the entire northern series of the Nations Championship through injury.

Connacht's Sean Jansen deputised in the first game of the November slate against Argentina but a knee injury ruled him out for the remainder of the autumn.

Nick Timoney moved from open-side flanker for the Fiji game before Sheehan was selected to face the back-to-back world champions.

Ireland have an otherwise full squad to choose from for the Wallabies game with head coach Andy Farrell to confirm his selection on Wednesday afternoon (16:00 GMT).

"That was a physical affair, as we knew it was going to be," said assistant coach Andrew Goodman of the victory over South Africa.

"Plenty of excitement and again, looking forward to a massive opportunity for the squad this week. We've got a full squad of fit bodies, which is great."

articles.title: England v New Zealand: Fin Smith on carrying hard and hosts' momentum
articles.summary: Fin Smith is only 5ft 10in tall and less than 14 stone, but the fly-half has become one of England's most prolific ball carriers.
articles.body:
With a grin and an expletive, Fin Smith describes Ben Earl as "greedy".

"It takes some doing to get just one carry when he's on the pitch," jokes Smith to BBC Sport. "He hogs them all."

Earl's performance in Saturday's win over New Zealand certainly caught the eye. The number eight carried a phenomenal 32 times in the 37-12 victory, more than twice as much as anyone else on the pitch.

But, further down the standings, Smith also stood out. He carried the ball 11 times against the All Blacks, the third-highest total of any England player.

That stat comes with context. The fly-half racked up his total in just 55 minutes on the pitch before cramp forced him to the bench.

For Smith, 5ft 10in tall and less than 14 stone, such physicality is not unusual.

A fortnight before beating New Zealand, against Australia, he carried nine times, his team's fourth-highest total.

According to stats from Oval Insights, he has carried more than any other fly-half in a Six Nations side this year.

If you include Rugby Championship teams in the mix, only three fly-halves - New Zealand's Richie Mo'unga, South Africa's Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and Argentina's Tomas Albornoz - have backed themselves more with the ball.

Smith admits he does not have the athletic ability of some of those rivals.

But the Northampton man says his attempts to play through the defence, rather than in front of them, helps him lead the team to a more effective attack.

"I do like the physical side," he adds. "It gets me into games, but also I think it is just my character.

"I would hate to be someone that is asking everyone else to go and be physical and put their body on the line, if I wasn't particularly willing to do it. I think that's how I've been brought up."

With George Furbank, Henry Slade and Seb Atkinson all able to step in at first receiver, Smith being buried at the bottom of the breakdown is a price England are able to pay for a phase or two.

"It's important for me to be a threat myself," he adds.

"The way we're playing at Northampton and England, and the way I feel like teams attack best when I'm in them, is when there are almost no numbers on backs.

"You play as quickly as possible and whoever ends up in the slots just does that job. You've got to be interchangeable.

"If the right thing to do is carry or the right thing to do is hit the breakdown then so be it, and then someone else can drop in as the first playmaker.

"I think that just makes us a harder team to play against. Our scrum-halves are running a lot more than they have and all of a sudden defences have got to think about do they tighten up to defend the nine and then if the 10s are running the ball a bit more they have to think about me.

"Then spaces open up and you've become so much less predictable."

After a miserable Six Nations, England have found a new attacking edge in the Nations Championship. They have scored 44 tries across their six games in the tournament, 10 more than any other side.

On Saturday, they are hunting a sixth-straight win as they face a rematch against New Zealand in the final's weekend's third-place play-off.

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app

Smith says England's current streak, after the five straight defeats that preceded it, has coincided with the team becoming more introspective, both on and off the pitch.

"The big thing that's changed would be we've been a lot more inwardly focused," Smith said.

"We're confident that if we're at our best, it should hopefully take care of whatever the opposition brings to the table.

"I think that was a big learning we got from the South Africa game [July's 45-21 defeat] is actually 'let's just do what we want to do and do it really well'.

"Standing on the pitch after we'd lost in Rome [to Italy in the Six Nations in March] was not that long ago and that's probably as low as I've been in my career.

"To now beating the All Blacks and playing well against Australia... just wanting to end the year on a good note is a massive one for for us and me this weekend.

"I've honestly absolutely loved these last few weeks from the feel around the training ground to the meetings, to the way we're training hard for each other, to dinners we're having in the evenings and then what we then put on the pitch.

"It's been as enjoyable a rugby experience as I can remember for a long time."

After the New Zealand rematch concludes their autumn campaign, England's next matches will be in the Six Nations where they travel to Ireland in the opening round on 5 February, before facing defending champions France the following weekend.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Citing hearing was 'extra stress' for Sam Prendergast before South Africa Test
articles.summary: Ireland's Sam Prendergast says head coach Andy Farrell was "unbelievably supportive" while the fly-half waited to find out whether he would be available to face South Africa last weekend.
articles.body:
Ireland's Sam Prendergast has said head coach Andy Farrell was "unbelievably supportive" while the fly-half waited to find out whether he would be available to face South Africa last weekend.

The Leinster playmaker had a citing complaint against him dismissed before starting in the 20-17 victory over the back-to-back world champions, but the alleged hip-drop tackle was brought up in media conferences by Springbok coaches Rassie Erasmus and Mzwandile Stick.

After the game, Farrell said he had not liked the comments made by his South African counterparts.

"It was a little bit hard," Prendergast said of facing a hearing during the build-up to such an important match.

"In terms of you're preparing for the game, but you also have that in the back of your mind - 'will I be playing?'

"After meeting with everyone at the start of the week, we felt pretty confident in the case. It added a little bit of extra stress, but that was early in the week.

"Once I got it out of the way it was pretty easy just to focus on the game."

Despite winning five of their six games in the Nations Championship, Ireland finished third in the northern hemisphere table.

They will finish the competition against Australia on Friday night (20:10 GMT) in what is expected to be a sparsely attended fixture in Twickenham.

Prendergast, however, believes Ireland will put just as much into the game as they did against South Africa.

"All I know is that we'll be taking it incredibly seriously," he added.

"We've taken every game as it comes this autumn, in terms of first game up [against Argentina], and then Fiji were such a tough Test.

"Last week was obviously a huge game, but I think this week is just as big."

articles.title: Beauden Barrett: All Blacks great close to stunning Bristol Bears move
articles.summary: New Zealand great Beauden Barrett is close to agreeing a deal to join Bristol Bears in what would be one of the highest-profile signings in Prem history.
articles.body:
New Zealand great Beauden Barrett is close to agreeing a deal to join Bristol Bears in what would be one of the highest-profile signings in Prem history.

The 35-year-old, who is widely considered one of the best All Blacks of all time, won his 150th international cap in Saturday's defeat by England in Twickenham.

It is understood he is in discussions about joining Bristol on a two-year deal after the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

Barrett is also the subject of interest from clubs in France as he plots the final stages of his illustrious career. An announcement on his future is expected in the coming weeks.

Bristol have yet to comment on the situation, but sources close to the deal feel the Bears are in a strong position to sign the 2015 World Cup winner .

New Zealand's international season finishes this weekend with a rematch against England in the Nations Championship third-place play-off (Saturday, 16:40 GMT).

As a new addition to the Prem, Barrett's salary would sit outside the cap as a designated marquee player.

While he will be 36 after next year's World Cup in Australia, Bristol are confident the back still has plenty to offer both on and off the field.

Barrett came through the ranks at Wellington-based Hurricanes, before joining the Blues in 2020, while he has also had stints in Japanese club rugby.

A move abroad after the World Cup would close the door on All Blacks selection, with eligibility rules preventing New Zealand from picking overseas-based players.

He would leave as one of the greatest All Blacks in history, and is closing in on Sam Whitelock's all-time caps record (153).

Bristol have made a handful of big-name signings in the past, such as New Zealand and Tonga winger Charles Piutau and Fiji talisman Semi Radradra.

If the signing is completed, Barrett would link up with Wales superstar Louis Rees-Zammit in the Bears backline.

articles.title: St Helens coach Kevin Walters insists he can win a trophy in his first season in charge and wants to restore team's winning DNA
articles.summary: New St Helens coach Kevin Walters has pinpointed where he believes things may have gone wrong for the club in 2026; St Helens missed the Super League play-offs for the first time in the club's history; Walters put pen to paper on a three-year deal in August
articles.body:
After guiding Australia to their fourth consecutive Rugby League World Cup success earlier this month, the former Brisbane Broncos boss has been tasked with galvanising the Saints following an underwhelming season that saw them slump to seventh in Super League and miss the play-offs for the first time in the club's history.

The 59-year-old, who put pen to paper on a three-year deal with the Saints in August, is confident he can restore the club to where it belongs and added St Helens are "not in as bad a position as some people may think".

Asked by Sky Sports Rugby League's Jenna Brooks whether he can win silverware in his first season, Walters said: "If I say no to that question, I look like a loser. I'm not a loser. I love winning.

"So I'm going to answer that positively and say yeah, I believe we can have great success here.

"It starts early; the pressure is on. I've been at big clubs and I understand the pressure that comes with it. I understand there's a lot of pressure on myself and the club to do well. But I'm confident we can do really well.

"Pressure is a privilege, isn't it? I wouldn't be in the role if I didn't [have that] understanding. There's always pressure in professional sport, particularly in rugby league - in Australia and here in the Super League. It's a big sport in the north.

"Everyone knows about St Helens and their success, and we need to get them back to where they belong."

It was a turbulent season for the 10-time Super League Grand Final winners, who suffered a swathe of injuries to key players, including Matty Lees and Jack Welsby, which contributed to their disappointing form.

St Helens also underwent some major coaching upheavals, with head coach Paul Rowley departing in May, less than a year into his three-year contract, before Eamon O'Carroll took over on an interim basis.

Club chiefs then turned to Walters, one of rugby league's most distinguished coaches. It will mark the first time the 59-year-old has taken up a full-time coaching role since he was sacked by the Brisbane Broncos in September 2024.

Walters reveals why he's the man for the job

Walters, who arrived in the United Kingdom on Monday and has already led a few training sessions with his new team, pinpoints a loss of connection between his players and fans as one of the side's biggest issues.

"It's hard to judge from afar. I've been speaking to people in the club; the connection between the team and the community is one thing that has been lost a little bit," Walters said.

"The Saints fans, from what I've seen and been told, are very passionate about their club. The English fans, across all of the teams, their passion is a little bit different to the Australian fans, who are probably not as vocal in their support, but also in their care for the side.

"I know there were some things that did go wrong; maybe the connection among the players was lost a little bit as well."

Walters, who also spearheaded Melbourne Storm's 2012 NRL Grand Final win, and won back-to-back State of Origin series as Queensland head coach in 2016 and 2017, believes he is the right man to solve that connectivity issue.

"One of my great strengths as a coach is my ability to bring people together for a common cause, and that's what I feel coaching is. Lots of things go into coaching; my ability to bring players and teams together, that's where I feel my big strength is.

"If I can do that here… well, I will do that here and then we'll see where that takes us."

He added: "Without making too many bold predictions, we're going to be hard to beat. That's the mainstay for me. Defensively, we've spoken to our players about getting better in that space.

"The last time Saints won the premiership in 2022, it was based on defence. We have to make sure we have a strong defensive team that's well connected and then when we get the ball, we're going to play some footy.

"The best defensive teams are there where it matters."

Reports have suggested that Tristan Sailor is being eyed up as a potential target for multiple other Super League clubs.

The full-back, who previously played under Walters at the Broncos, joined the Saints in August 2024 and has gone on to make 54 appearances for the club.

While Welsby is favoured to lock down the No 1 jumper for St Helens, Walters insisted Sailor still has a future at the club.

"There's a lot of noise around the whole group and Tristan has been caught up in that," Walters said. "I believe Tristan's got a lot to offer this club still.

"He's been a great player here. I coached him at the Broncos and unfortunately Reece Walsh was parked in front of him in that role at full-back.

"He's come here in a different role, but I feel Tristan... whatever position he plays - he was good playing full-back, centre, five-eighth, he might have played some wing. Mr Versatility but also a very good team person."

articles.title: England vs New Zealand: Greg Fisilau starts as Steve Borthwick makes five changes for Nations Championship rematch
articles.summary: Steve Borthwick has made five changes to England's starting XV for the Nations Championship third-place play-off against New Zealand; England face the All Blacks for the second weekend running after beating them by a record 25 points in their 37-12 victory at Twickenham on Saturday
articles.body:
The more defensive-minded Freddie Steward replaces George Furbank, who started at full-back in England's 37-12 victory against the same opposition - their record margin of victory against the All Blacks.

Exciting back-rower Greg Fisilau, who impressed off the bench during England's 78-15 demolition of Japan , will make his first international start, as he replaces Ben Curry at openside flanker.

In the forwards, Ellis Genge comes in for Fin Baxter at prop, while Luke Cowan-Dickie replaces Jamie George at hooker.

Winger Tommy Freeman was ruled out of last weekend's win shortly before kick-off after pulling up with a quad issue, but returns to the starting line-up in place of Cadan Murley on Saturday.

No 10 Fin Smith was spotted applying ice to his legs after being substituted last weekend. However, having recovered from cramp, he has retained his place in the starting XV, while Henry Pollock remains on the bench.

England will be aiming to deliver another impressive performance and secure third place in the inaugural Nations Championship, following their emphatic victory over New Zealand in their previous outing. The match comes a day before France take on South Africa at Twickenham in the tournament final.

England's commanding win over the All Blacks has also had a significant impact on the world rankings. Borthwick's side have climbed from fifth to fourth, while New Zealand have dropped from second to fifth.
