articles.title: England v New Zealand: Greg Fisilau and Freddie Steward in hosts' XV
articles.summary: Exeter back row Greg Fisilau will make his first England start in one of five changes to their XV to face New Zealand on Saturday.
articles.body:
Hard-hitting back row Greg Fisilau will make his first England start in one of five changes to their XV to face New Zealand.

The Plymouth-born 23-year-old, whose father Keni was a Tonga international, has impressed off the bench in each of England's previous three wins this autumn.

He brings an industrious carrying option to a back row that relies heavily on Ben Earl in that aspect of the game. Ben Curry's breakdown skills have been sacrificed to make space, with the Sale man relegated to the bench.

Exeter's Fisilau has carried more than any other player in the Prem this season, as well as sitting fourth in the top-flight's tackle standings.

Elsewhere Freddie Steward's good form is rewarded with an opportunity ahead of George Furbank at full-back, while Tommy Freeman returns on the wing for Saturday's rematch (16:40 GMT).

Freeman missed last weekend's 37-12 victory over the All Blacks with a minor thigh issue which forced his withdrawal in the hours before kick-off.

Ellis Genge comes into the starting front row after a string of barnstorming performances across the latter half of England's Nations Championship campaign.

He is joined in the front row by Luke Cowan-Dickie, who is preferred at hooker to Jamie George.

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app

Northampton's 21-year-old scrum-half Archie McParland, who made his debut off the bench against Japan a fortnight ago, is among the replacements once again.

With less than a year until the Rugby World Cup, England head coach Steve Borthwick's auditions for fringe squad members are taking on more importance.

Victory would ensure an autumn clean sweep, a sixth win in succession and a third-place finish in the overall standings of the inaugural Nations Championship.

A win would also contribute to the northern hemisphere's points tally in a Ryder Cup-style competition which runs throughout the three days of action at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

The tournament is being held every other year between Rugby World Cups and British and Irish Lions tours in an attempt to bring more of a narrative to the Test calendar and draw in fans.

Six Nations holders France and world champions South Africa will contest Sunday's grand final (16:40 GMT).

England XV: Steward; Freeman, Slade, Atkinson, Joseph; F Smith, Van Poortvliet; Genge, Cowan-Dickie, Heyes, Itoje (c), Coles, Chessum, G Fisilau, Earl

Replacements: George, Baxter, Stuart, Martin, B Curry, Pollock, McParland, M Smith

When Fisilau first broke through at Exeter, a story emerged that his father banned him from playing touch rugby as a boy as he was concerned that it would teach him habits contrary to a traditional Pacific Islands physicality.

It turned out a clash with the family's church commitments was actually the motivation for Greg missing mini rugby.

Either way, Fisilau has certainly retained his explosive power, with several juddering hits, particularly against Japan, added to his highlight reel this autumn.

"It is clear the power and physicality he brings," said Borthwick.

"I think Greg adds in that area. We've seen him do it off the bench. And now I want to see him do it from the start of the game.

"He has grabbed his chance and taken it with both hands. I'm delighted for him, delighted for his family. His dad always said, until he plays for England, his dad's the best rugby player in the family. Well, Greg's now the best rugby player in the family, and I think he's very proud of it."

Borthwick added Fisilau would also be tasked with contesting the breakdown, where New Zealand, who won six turnovers to England's five last week, managed to get a toehold in Saturday's game.

"Greg has got an engine that is out of this world, and we're going to need that," said Borthwick. "We're going to need him in that breakdown presence, so that's why I preferred him at seven and keeping Ben Earl consistent at eight."

In bringing in Steward, who is a tall, rangy runner with great aerial ability rather than a playmaker in the mould of Furbank, Borthwick has made a stylistic change at full-back.

"They definitely have some different strengths," Borthwick said of his options at 15.

"I think Fred's carrying through the line is very significant, that little bit more power to create some more dent as well.

"He's really stepped up with his link play on edges, which has been very good. He has chased improvement. Everyone talks so much about his high-ball strength but there was always more to his game in that.

"He's also added the real effectiveness to his defence. Everyone knew he also had the long kicking game, but he's added that short kicking game.

"He deserves enormous praise for continuing to build his game."

Borthwick said that England's 2019 Rugby World Cup campaign, in which they lost to South Africa in the final after a superb 19-7 victory over New Zealand a week earlier, is informing their preparation for Saturday.

Borthwick was an assistant coach to predecessor Eddie Jones at the time. Jones subsequently said he regretted not making more changes to his line-up for the showpiece game - specifically not bringing in Joe Marler and Henry Slade to face the Springboks.

"It's certainly been a consideration, without question," said Borthwick of his 2019 experience.

"I was there then, and part of that review, and it was something we spoke about in the review. Trying to find the right balance, making the right number of changes and the right changes, is key.

"There's a freshness to the players, a number of them that want to come in, want to get their hands on the ball, and really take the game forward."

articles.title: Ireland v Australia: Jacob Stockdale returns as Irish make two changes for Nations Championship fifth-place play-off
articles.summary: Ulster wing Jacob Stockdale is recalled to the Ireland starting team for Friday night's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off match against Australia.
articles.body:
Ulster wing Jacob Stockdale has been recalled to the Ireland line-up for Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off match against Australia.

Stockdale, who was not involved in Ireland's home wins over Argentina, Fiji and South Africa, replaces Mack Hansen on the left wing.

Nick Timoney comes in for Dan Sheehan at number eight in the only other change to the line-up that started Saturday's 20-17 victory over world champions South Africa at Aviva Stadium.

Sheehan is ruled out of Friday's match at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium (20:10 GMT) after being banned for two games for a croc-roll tackle during the victory over the Springboks.

Tadhg Beirne will captain Ireland in Sheehan's absence for the second time this autumn, having also stepped up against Fiji when Sheehan was ruled out through concussion.

Sheehan out of Wallabies Test after two-game ban

South Africa win 'sets us up nicely' - Farrell

Did Springboks win change the narrative for Ireland?

Stockdale returns to the line-up for his 44th cap after a strong start to the season with Ulster, with three tries in as many games.

The 30-year-old started Ireland's Six Nations defeat by France in Paris in February, and while he was not picked against Italy or England, he made a try-scoring return against Wales.

Friday will be Stockdale's first appearance in green since July's Nations Championship victory over Japan.

He is one of eight Ulster players in head coach Andy Farrell's matchday squad. Robert Baloucoune, who starred with two tries against the Springboks, is retained at right wing with Stuart McCloskey kept at inside centre.

With Sheehan out, Timoney returns to number eight. Farrell is dealing with an injury crisis in the back-row position with Caelan Doris, Jack Conan and Sean Jansen ruled out.

Timoney started at the base of the scrum against Fiji having been preferred to Josh van der Flier at open-side flanker for the Argentina game.

Hooker Tom Stewart and prop Tom O'Toole are retained on the bench alongside Leinster's Thomas Clarkson, who have been dubbed the 'Tom Squad'.

James McNabney is back among the replacements after his eye-catching debut against Fiji was cut short by a concussion.

Nathan Doak, who like Stockdale has not been involved so far this month, is named as the back-up scrum-half.

Despite a taxing win over South Africa, Farrell has opted against making wholesale changes with Andrew Porter, Ronan Kelleher and Tadhg Furlong retained in the front row.

Joe McCarthy and Beirne are kept in the second row with Ryan Baird and Van der Flier alongside Timoney in the back row.

Despite a morale-boosting win over South Africa to round out the Nations Championship campaign with five wins from six games, Ireland finished third in the northern hemisphere standings behind France and England.

Australia finished third in the southern hemisphere table behind South Africa and New Zealand despite losing four of their six games, including a 33-31 defeat by Ireland in the opening round in Sydney.

Since that game, Joe Schmidt has been replaced as Wallabies boss by former Ireland defence coach and Ulster director of rugby Les Kiss.

Kiss has named two uncapped players in his matchday squad with James Ramm selected on the left wing and Teddy Wilson - son of former World Cup winner David - named as the replacement scrum-half.

The Wallabies bench also features 37-year-old utility back Kurtley Beale, who is set to earn his first cap in five years.

Allan Alaalatoa will co-captain the Wallabies on his 100th cap alongside Harry Wilson, who is named on the bench, while scrum-half Kalani Thomas earns his first Test start after coming off the bench in last weekend's win over Wales in Cardiff.

articles.title: Ireland vs Australia: Mack Hansen out with injury as Nick Timoney replaces suspended Dan Sheehan for Nations Championship clash
articles.summary: Ireland have been forced into making two changes ahead of their Nations Championship clash against Australia on Friday; Andy Farrell's side will be without Dan Sheehan after he was suspended; Mack Hansen has been ruled out with an injury
articles.body:
Andy Farrell has been forced to make two changes to the side that beat South Africa 20-17 last Saturday, with Ulster's Jacob Stockdale being handed a surprise return as he steps in for Hansen.

Stockdale hasn't featured for Ireland at all during the Northern Hemisphere series, with Hansen featuring in all three of Ireland's Autumn Tests.

Dan Sheehan was suspended for two matches after he had a yellow card for a croc-roll against South Africa upgraded to a red card.

Sheehan had started at No 8 for Saturday's epic win in Dublin and will be replaced by loose forward Nick Timoney, who came on to play the final 20 minutes of that match.

On the bench, Farrell has made a further two changes with James McNabney replacing Timoney on the bench, while Nathan Doak comes in for Craig Casey.

Meanwhile, Australia head coach Les Kiss has made several changes to his starting XV, with uncapped James Ramm set to replace Harry Potter on the left wing.

Taniela Tupou, who started against Wales, moves to the bench, with Allan Alaalatoa taking over at tighthead prop. Alaalatoa will also captain Australia in what will be his 100th appearance for the Wallabies.

Tom Hooper moves to blindside flanker, with Jeremy Williams stepping into the second row, while Rob Valetini shifts to No 8 in place of Harry Wilson, who drops to the bench.

Ryan Lonergan replaces Kalani Thomas at scrum-half.

"He is a talismanic figure within the group, and I know the whole squad and support staff will be doing everything they can to make this rare milestone a memorable one for him, his family and for us," Kiss said of Alaalatoa.

"We've taken some steps forward, grown our game and tested our squad depth this year as a squad and I know the team is highly motivated to put in a performance that reflects the hard work put in by everyone in our final Test."

articles.title: Wales v Japan: Steve Tandy to tinker team for Nations Championship finale
articles.summary: Wales head coach Steve Tandy will tinker with his side to face Japan in the Nations Championship finale at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Saturday (13:10 GMT).
articles.body:
Wales head coach Steve Tandy will tinker with his side to face Japan in the Nations Championship finale at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Saturday (13:10 GMT).

Scrum-half Tomos Williams, who has started 14 out of 15 matches under Tandy, including the past 11, is battling to shake off a groin injury that forced him off early in the second half against Australia.

If Williams is ruled out, Reuben Morgan-Williams could make his first Wales first start, while Dragons' number nine Che Hope would be in line to win his first cap off the bench.

Hooker Ryan Elias could also start with Tandy considering rotating and not starting captain Dewi Lake and British and Irish Lions flanker Jac Morgan.

Flanker James Botham is in line for a return after missing the 29-26 defeat against Australia, while Taine Plumtree could be handed a start after two replacement appearances.

Scarlets wing Ellis Mee will be hoping for his first match-day involvement after missing the three games so far in November.

Tandy will name his team on Thursday at 09:00 GMT as Wales face Eddie Jones’ Japan for a fifth time in 16 months after both sides finished fifth in their respective sections.

The Wales coach says there will be members of the 39-strong Nations Championship squad who will not have game time this month.

“There will be changes but there won't be wholesale changes,” said Tandy.

“We want to build cohesion and as a back line we are starting to come together.

“We want to keep building momentum and performances.

“Some boys will get an opportunity and unfortunately some boys won't which is always tough going through a campaign when people have done such great jobs.

“All the boys that have been involved have been fantastic, but ultimately it's for us to build momentum and keep building on performances.”

articles.title: Nations Championship: Ireland head coach Andy Farrell's side against Australia out to 'back up' South Africa win
articles.summary: Ireland head coach Andy Farrell believes the Nations Championship can be good preparation for next year's World Cup.
articles.body:
Ireland head coach Andy Farrell believes the Nations Championship can be good preparation for next year's World Cup.

With his side facing Australia in the fifth-place play-off on Friday night (20:10 GMT), Farrell has made just two changes to the starting team that beat South Africa last weekend with the injured Mack Hansen and banned Dan Sheehan missing out.

Having resisted any urge to rotate his selection, Farrell wants to build on the momentum of last week's big win and those over Fiji and Argentina that preceded it.

"Well, I mean, four games on the bounce and being able to perform in those four games, it's pretty important for what we've got coming up," he said.

"Five games in the Six Nations and then, if you've got any ambition, you're trying to play six or seven in the World Cup.

"These tournaments are there to be used in the right manner and we've got to back up in a six-day turnaround what was a decent enough performance last week."

The 20-17 victory over the back-to-back world champions has shifted the narrative around Ireland, who before Saturday had endured six consecutive double-digit losses to South Africa, France and New Zealand.

Less than a year out from the World Cup, Farrell does not mind his side remaining "under the radar" compared to the group that went to France 2023 ranked number one in the world.

"We're at different stages because of personnel and people in key positions gaining experience," he added.

"There's been plenty of firsts last year and we've learned from all them.

"It's not a bad place to be, a little bit under the radar, but we've still got ambitions to get on that plane with a lot of belief behind us."

articles.title: Nations Championship: Steve Borthwick says England's All Blacks Tests 'World Cup practice' | Andy Farrell: Ireland still aren't World Cup contenders
articles.summary: Final weekend of Nations Championship takes place at Allianz Stadium; Ireland vs Australia on Friday (8.10pm), England vs New Zealand on Saturday (4.40pm), France vs South Africa in final on Sunday (4.40pm); coaches Steve Borthwick, Andy Farrell and Dave Rennie speak to media
articles.body:
England, having come into the tournament under a cloud of pressure following the worst Six Nations display in their history earlier this year (four losses, fifth place), have stormed to victories over Australia, Japan and New Zealand this month.

Last week, Borthwick's side secured a record 25-point victory over the All Blacks at Allianz Stadium. With England finishing second behind France in the northern hemisphere standings and New Zealand runners-up to South Africa in the southern hemisphere table, the two sides are now set for an immediate rematch.

England face the All Blacks again at Twickenham on Saturday, with Borthwick viewing the latest clash as valuable preparation for the Rugby World Cup in Australia in 10 months' time.

"The nature of this tournament, it's a new tournament, is the understanding that international games have that level of jeopardy," Borthwick told the media on Wednesday.

"The consequence upon each of these games. This is an important step.

"It's a real positive step in this competition towards the jeopardy of being involved in World Cup games.

"In the World Cup, you want to be in situations where you're having to back up big games in multiple weeks.

"I think it's going to be an excellent Test match this weekend, a really tough Test match against a super dangerous New Zealand team.

"We're expecting New Zealand to come hard at the breakdown, and we're expecting them to really challenge us there.

"All our focus this weekend is we're expecting the very best of New Zealand. They're full of so much talent and so much experience. We know this is going to be a fierce Test match.

"We've got a young squad. We've got some players that are very experienced at the end of the spectrum and a lot of players that are young and haven't played against teams like New Zealand that often. So I think it was an important step in our development.

"This Saturday is another very important step. Each and every international experience we have is vital for the long-term development of this team."

Ireland's Farrell: We still aren't World Cup contenders despite win vs Springboks

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell began this Test window by telling the media that, unlike in 2023, this current Ireland side - based on performances to date - are not Rugby World Cup contenders.

What has followed this month is dominant victories over Argentina and Fiji in Dublin, followed by a stunning 20-17 success over double world champions South Africa last week.

Ireland face Australia at Twickenham on Friday, but Farrell reiterated his point that Ireland are not in World Cup-title conversations.

"No [Ireland are not World Cup contenders]," he said. "We took a step in the right direction last week, but that's got to continue to be that, hasn't it? To make sure that we keep feeling that way.

"That's always going to be the challenge [emotional challenge a week after win over Springboks].

"Plus, we have a six-day turnaround, and we play Scotland in the World Cup with a six-day turnaround as well. Getting yourself back up, that's the way you get some consistency in your performance, so it's pretty important.

"You are testing your depth, and you're always going to get that with four quality games over such a short space of time. But the Six Nations is five games, and then the World Cup is seven games if you've got any ambition, really.

"It's not ideal [shortage at No 8], but again, these are things that happen over a tournament, and that's what we've found this year.

"Obviously, from the start having so many experienced players in Caelan Doris and Jack Conan out - played plenty of times for us - and then we've lost a few as we've gone on.

"But you've got to be able to adapt with the squad that you've got, and you've been able to do that so far.

"It is what it is [Dan Sheehan's two-Test ban]. He had a fair hearing, and we move on."

All Blacks boss Rennie responds to calls for his sacking: 'Nature of the job'

New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie has overseen a first All Blacks defeat to Wales since 1953 and a record loss to England this month.

Such results have led to huge pressure and reports he should be sacked.

"I don't listen to anything. I don't read anything, so that probably helps," Rennie said.

"Look, it's the nature of the job, and it's the expectations of this role too.

"But international rugby now is really tight. You look at the recent results, and I think four years ago heading into a World Cup, Ireland and France were ranked No 1 and No 2, so things can change really quickly.

"It wasn't that long ago South Africa and us were No 1 and No 2. We're well aware of how tough it is, and England are a really good side.

"But we believe if we get our game right, we'll be competitive at the weekend.

"We're just excited to wear the jersey again and put on a performance that we're proud of and the country's proud of. We'll talk about fatigue next week.

"You want it to hurt, because we're all hurt after the weekend.

"Sunday's still a bit of a struggle, but you can't afford to sulk because you've got to look forward and think: 'How do we fix things?'

"Our job is to try and bring energy and connection and we're a really tight group. We want to get a result on the weekend for us, but also for the country.

"We're really appreciative of all the support we've got, especially after last week's performance. We're determined to rectify that."

articles.title: Nations Championship finals: Rice cookers, prosecco and unknowns
articles.summary: The unprecedented demands of Nations Championship finals weekend have been met by meticulous planning.
articles.body:
Earlier this year, when planning their Nations Championship finals week, Argentina's staff had a request.

Would their hotel in Shepperton allow the team to scorch a patch of the hotel garden for an asado – a traditional Argentine barbecue, in which meat on a low grill is cooked over a bed of hot charcoal?

Japan were also making arrangements. The Brave Blossoms had a special rice cooker shipped over to supplement the kitchen facilities at their Kensington base.

Such are the countless details that go into an unprecedented logistical juggle.

The Nations Championship brings together more than 550 players and support staff from the world's top 12 teams for six matches funnelled into three days and just one venue - Twickenham.

The new tournament has made new, unprecedented demands on organisers.

The first was to find enough accommodation in one corner of London, on a notoriously busy shopping weekend, kicked off by Black Friday sales.

A block booking was therefore made back at the start of the year to secure beds in hotels from Brentford, Guildford, Cobham and beyond.

Not all those establishments had experience of hosting elite rugby teams.

So, chefs and team nutritionists convened to ensure that the hotels were braced with sufficient supplies of eggs, chicken and the rest, to cater for the high-energy, high-protein diets of rugby's best players.

While their fellow hotel guests might hit the sights, Nations Championship sides hit the pitch.

Individual, private training facilities have had to be sourced for each team, with pitches hired out at local clubs, schools and universities.

Teams were given the choice of hotels and training grounds based on their world ranking at the start of the tournament in July, with world number ones South Africa nabbing the Teddington base that usually hosts England's opponents on a regular autumn internationals weekend.

The choice is all the more important given the logjam of matches means teams will do their eve-of-match captain's run session at their training ground, rather than, as traditional, at the match venue.

To get their players, staff and equipment between hotel, training base and Twickenham itself, organisers have given each team use of four vehicles; a team bus, a people carrier, a van for training kit and a truck for moving scrum machines and other heavy items.

Once they finally do arrive, Allianz Stadium, which has hosted Sevens, double-headers and schools finals days in the past, has enough changing rooms to comfortably accommodate four teams at once.

The higher-ranked team is given the home dressing room in each fixture.

Had England lost to New Zealand last weekend, they would be in the unfamiliar away dressing room. Victory however bumped them up to fourth, the All Blacks down to fifth and secured their usual spot.

Even if they dodge the traffic however, there is tunnel congestion to be dealt with.

The first match on each of the three days kicks off three and half hours before the headline fixture.

Barring extraordinary levels of intervention from the Television Match Official, the final whistle should blow in the first fixture before the team buses for those involved in the second arrive.

However, with post-match media duties, feeding and debriefing to be done, a window between five minutes and half an hour after kick-off in the second fixture has been identified for the teams involved in the first to make a hassle-free getaway.

Fisilau starts as England change five for All Blacks rematch

Botham back as Morgan-Williams to make first start

Ireland's Stockdale returns as Beale, 37, back for Wallabies

One team has asked for permission to break with protocol. Scotland's players may stay to watch the South Africa v France grand final (16:40 GMT) as a squad social event after their own play-off against Argentina on Sunday (13:10).

Twickenham's ground staff are confident that, despite forecast rain on Saturday, the Allianz Stadium pitch will still be in good shape by the sixth match in 48 hours.

What happens in the stands is less predictable.

"We sell out at 99.9% of England men's games and we have a very clear picture of what we need to order for those," says Nils Braude, the managing director of the Twickenham Experience.

Nations Championship finals weekend will be different. Filling the 82,000-capacity Allianz Stadium, with only a week's notice on which teams will be playing when, has proved trickier.

It is estimated that Italy v Fiji and Ireland v Australia - Friday's double-header - may play out to a half-full stadium.

Braude is dealing with different numbers, demographics and demands.

"If you are a member of the public that doesn't get to go to rugby very often, now is your chance to come in," he adds.

"We are anticipating it is going to be much more akin to a general event-goer or a Red Roses game, so a more family orientated, mixed generational crowd.

"That causes a bit more just thinking about what we order

"New fans generally arrive a bit earlier than a rugby fan who has their habits well established.

"The new fans tend to eat more, particularly if it's a long day. If they are arriving an hour or two before the first game and leaving an hour after the last game, they are here for a significant amount of time.

"So having enough food on site to satisfy that demand is a key.

"As for drinks, we're known for serving a lot of Guinness, and so we can always do that. But we are anticipating a crowd that tends to look for more cocktails, Proseccos, non-alcoholic drinks and soft drinks, so we do ramp those up a little bit for these type of games."

While the stadium's bars, which number close to 80, are loaded with enough drink to see out the first two days of the Nations Championship, there are beer kegs stored in the car parks around the stadium in place to fill any unexpected shortfall.

Equally Twickenham's partner breweries and suppliers are on alert to truck in more if required.

That restocking is part of a 24-hour operation that will be in place across the Nations Championship finals weekend.

Chefs tend to be first on site from around 05:00, with a central kitchen preparing meals for the stadium's hospitality suites. After the match has taken place and the crowd has cleared, the cleaning crew descend.

They will work through the stadium seat by seat in the couple of hours after the final whistle and then to concourses and removing empties, rubbish and hospitality table linen.

Deliveries happen overnight to take advantage of an empty venue and the clearer roads around it.

For a stadium keen to host more events throughout the year, it is also a chance to show its consideration for residential neighbours, even on compressed timeframes.

The crash of glass recycling and reversing beep of forklift trucks will be restricted to certain hours.

Braude is also keen to ensure his own team get the rest and recovery they need over a weekend that comes on the back of a busy autumn.

But alongside the challenges, there is an opportunity.

"It's exciting," says Braude. "It is certainly an event that shows up. You can really flex your muscles as a venue when you have these type of events."

Brawn and brain is being deployed well beyond the white lines this weekend.

articles.title: Wales v Japan: James Botham recalled as Reuben Morgan-Williams to make first start
articles.summary: Wales flanker James Botham is recalled by head coach Steve Tandy as one of five changes for the Nations Championship finale against Japan.
articles.body:
Wales flanker James Botham has been recalled by head coach Steve Tandy as one of five changes for the Nations Championship finale against Japan at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

In the only backline alteration for the game in Twickenham, Ospreys scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams will make his first Wales start, with Tomos Williams named among the replacements.

Exeter lock Dafydd Jenkins will captain the side for the first time in more than two years with regular skipper Dewi Lake and flanker Jac Morgan also dropping to the bench.

Prop Rhys Carre and hooker Ryan Elias make their first starts of the November campaign, while lock Adam Beard returns at the expense of Ben Carter.

Wales have named an experienced bench that includes 294 caps.

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra 2 on BBC Sounds

Botham produced a player-of-the-match display in the 35-28 victory against New Zealand after making 30 tackles but was left out of the 29-26 defeat by Australia in favour of Cardiff colleague Alex Mann.

It was a decision which Botham’s father Liam, himself a former Cardiff wing, said Tandy had got wrong.

“I know there's a lot been spoken about it,” said Tandy.

“Everyone has got their opinions and people generally tell you who should be in the team and they never tell you who shouldn't.

“We're a tight group and as a coach I make sure I speak to all the players before if they are not selected. There'll be reasons why, whether it be bigger picture or whether it is form.

“I'll always speak to those, that's a special thing and the connection we feel in our environment.”

Botham, who became a father earlier this week, will play at open-side flanker against Japan after starring at blind-side against the All Blacks, with Mann and number eight Aaron Wainwright completing the back row.

“James was outstanding against the All Blacks, but we've got a back row depth there that we can move things around and freshen things up," said Tandy.

“James has had his little one, he's coming back in full of energy. We were so pleased for him things have gone well there."

Wales need strong finish to campaign - Morgan

A world-class winger - Louis Rees-Zammit 2.0

Chance for Morgan-Williams to shine at nine

Ospreys number nine Morgan-Williams is preparing for his first start in a position that has been dominated by Saracens scrum-half Williams during the Tandy era.

Williams has started 14 out of the 15 internationals, including the previous 11, with opportunities in short supply for others. But Williams came off early in the second half against Australia with a groin problem.

Carre, named Welsh rugby writers player of the 2025-26 season, is given his first start this autumn, with Nicky Smith dropping out of the squad.

Saracens loose-head Carre missed the first month of the season because of a hamstring injury and his only appearance of the autumn Tests so far was off the bench against Japan.

Elias, a replacement in the three previous November internationals, is handed his first Test start since the 2024 Six Nations match against France.

Montpellier lock Beard returns after missing the loss to Australia after suffering a shoulder injury against New Zealand.

Scarlets wing Ellis Mee is given his first involvement in the campaign after being named as a replacement.

Tandy has settled on his backline with full-back Blair Murray, wing Louis Rees-Zammit, centres Eddie James and Max Llewellyn and fly-half Sam Costelow starting all four matches in the November campaign as well as prop Archie Griffin and Jenkins.

Uncapped quartet Che Hope, Macs Page, Rhys Barratt and Aneurin Owen are among the players who will not be given game time, alongside Liam Belcher, Tom Rogers and Seb Davies, while Keiron Assiratti and Jarrod Evans have been late call-ups.

Wales have won three and lost three of their six Nations Championship matches to finish fifth in the northern hemisphere group, a position matched by Japan in the southern hemisphere section.

Wales will face Eddie Jones’ Japan side for a fifth time inside two years with Wales winning three out of the four games.

It is the first match of a Saturday double-header, with England and New Zealand to follow.

“We were frustrated and disappointed with losing last weekend,” said Tandy.

“We probably weren't as accurate as we could have been but there were a lot of positives in the performance to take also.

“We want to go out there, be ruthless and show improvement on our previous performance against Japan."

Wales: Murray: Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Adams: Costelow, Morgan-Williams; Carre, Elias, Griffin, D Jenkins (capt), Beard, Mann, Botham, Wainwright.

Replacements: Lake, G Thomas, Lewis, Plumtree, J Morgan, Tomos Williams, Hawkins, Mee.

articles.title: All Blacks star Beauden Barrett in talks to join Bristol Bears after 2027 Rugby World Cup
articles.summary: Beauden Barrett has had interest from multiple northern hemisphere clubs, including some in France's Top 14; the 35-year-old became only the second All Blacks player to reach 150 caps during his side's Nations Championship defeat by England on Saturday
articles.body:
The 35-year-old, who became only the second All Black to reach 150 international caps during England's 37-12 victory over New Zealand on Saturday, is also reportedly attracting interest from clubs in France's Top 14.

Should he put pen to paper on a deal with the Bears, he would likely become the club's marquee signing, meaning his wages would sit outside of Bristol's salary cap.

It would be one of the most significant acquisitions in Prem history, with Barrett, who can play at both fly-half and full-back, revered as one of the All Blacks' greatest players.

The 2015 Rugby World Cup winner is the fourth most-capped player in international rugby history and, for the All Blacks, ranks second for most tries and third for most points scored.

Barrett began his Super Rugby career playing for the Hurricanes in 2011, and after winning the Super Rugby championship in 2015, he moved to the Blues. He has played for the Auckland-based club since.

In recent years, Barrett also enjoyed spells with Japanese sides Tokyo Sungoliath in 2021 and Toyota Verblitz in 2023.

A move to the northern hemisphere would present a great opportunity for Barrett, who will be 36 after the 2027 Rugby World Cup and is unlikely to represent his country after that tournament.

As part of the All Blacks selection requirements, players must generally be contracted to a team in New Zealand to represent the All Blacks, and a move to Europe could likely end his international career.

He would not be the first of the Barrett brothers to play for a European club. His younger brother, Jordie, signed a short-term deal with Leinster in December 2024.

Barrett's potential arrival at Bristol would bolster an already dangerous backline which includes the likes of Benhard Janse van Rensburg, Gabriel Ibitoye and Louis Rees-Zammit.

articles.title: Nigel Starmer-Smith: Former England international and commentator dies aged 81
articles.summary: Former England international and rugby union commentator Nigel Starmer-Smith dies aged 81.
articles.body:
Former England scrum-half and rugby union commentator Nigel Starmer-Smith has died aged 81.

He had been diagnosed with dementia in 2015.

Starmer-Smith represented Harlequins and the Barbarians, and made seven appearances for England between 1969-71.

After his retirement in 1976, Starmer-Smith moved into broadcasting and journalism.

He voiced the BBC's highlights programme Rugby Special for 15 years and commentated for ITV at the 2003 World Cup in Australia, won by England.

Starmer-Smith's son Charlie spoke about his father's condition in 2021, saying dementia was a "big issue" in sport and describing how the family were only able to see him through the window during the Covid-19 pandemic.

He said that getting knocked out in a game of rugby was "like a badge of honour" during his father's playing days but also said dementia ran in their family, with his uncle also dying from the disease.

"Dad passed away peacefully this morning after a long battle with dementia," Charlie posted on social media on Thursday.

"He was (as they say in rugby circles) one of life's great tourists. A rugby player, commentator, editor, writer, raconteur, charity fundraiser, volunteer, speaker, prankster, family man, life and soul of the party, but, above all, the greatest father anyone could wish to have.

"He did everything for us and, despite having to bury two of his children at cruelly young ages, both he and my Mum refused to let the cavernous holes that Charlotte and Julian left behind define them.

"Just as I choose not to let the cruel condition that robbed him of his ability to communicate (and ultimately of his dignity), define my memories of him.

"He was a modest man and he'd hate for people to make a fuss. He loved to laugh but not as much as he loved to see others laughing. So for those that knew him think of a happy memory and smile. For that's how I'll remember him."

The BBC paid tribute to Starmer-Smith, with head of sport, Philip Bernie, saying: Nigel was a very distinguished commentator for the BBC after his successful rugby playing days.

"His enthusiasm and love for the game always shone through in his excellent, engaging broadcasting across so many great matches he memorably called, and for Rugby Special.

"All our thoughts and sympathies are with his family and those closest to him."

articles.title: No post-match drug testing in South Africa v New Zealand series
articles.summary: No post-match samples was taken from South Africa and New Zealand players during their four-Test series earlier this year.
articles.body:
South Africa and New Zealand players were not subjected to a single post-match drugs test by anti-doping authorities when they contested this year's Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.

The four-Test series, played in August and September, is a new biennial initiative between the two southern hemisphere powerhouses aimed at boosted revenues and profiles.

An agreement over how the series operates refers to World Rugby anti-doping rules; but, in practice, post-match tests, which are standard practice at most elite-level matches, were not carried out.

Players in the series could have been tested by either of two official bodies.

All players involved in the series are part of World Rugby's testing pool. The global governing body conducts on-the-spot tests on top players around the world throughout the year.

The South African Institute for Drug-Free Sport (Saids) runs its own domestic anti-doping programme, covering sporting events and athletes in the country.

With all matches, bar the fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore, taking place in South Africa, Saids could have demanded samples from players after games.

World Rugby would not confirm the lack of post-match testing in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series, but it stressed that all players are subject to the "always-on" testing regime.

"World Rugby operates a risk-based no-notice anti-doping programme in line with the World Anti-Doping Agency code," said a spokesperson.

"All qualified men's and women's Rugby World Cup team players are included within a dedicated out-of-competition testing pool which is not competition specific.

"This means that all these players are subject to testing on a no-notice, any location basis throughout the calendar year, including within international competition windows.

"This means that over the course of the year, both teams are tested in and out of competition in line with World Rugby's programme and are also subject to testing undertaken by the respective national anti-doping agencies at both the international and domestic/cross border club levels."

Saids referred queries about testing in Rugby's Greatest Rivalry back to World Rugby, saying the global body had "jurisdiction" over the matches.

The latest figures from the World Anti-Doping Agency show there were 9,583 accredited doping tests in rugby union globally in 2024, with 0.6% coming back positive.

That number of tests is fewer than those conducted in athletics (44,044), cycling (26,156), aquatics (17,447), but more than in wrestling (7,620), triathlon, (4,478) and gymnastics (4,190).

The number of rugby players tested by Saids has fallen significantly in recent years.

The most recent Saids annual report, covering the 12 months to 31 March, records 225 tests in the sport.

A decade before, the equivalent number was 753.

UK Anti-Doping, which covers England, Scotland and Wales, carried out 1,086 tests in rugby union in 2025. New Zealand's Sport Integrity Commission conducted 249 tests in rugby over the same period.

Currently two rugby union players in New Zealand – both well below elite level – are serving suspensions for doping.

The cost of testing has dramatically increased for Saids after the World Anti-Doping Agency revoked its accreditation for a sample-testing laboratory in Bloemfontein in May 2025. , external

With no other such facilities in Africa, Saids has to send samples long distances for testing. It says its budget has been hit by foreign currency costs from overseas laboratories, courier costs and import charges.

While elsewhere violations have mainly been restricted to players outside the elite, the Springboks have been hit by several doping cases in recent years.

Aphiwe Dyantyi, who made 13 appearances for the team and was named as World Rugby's breakthrough player of 2018, was banned for four years after he tested positive for a cocktail of steroids.

Sbu Nkosi and Elton Jantjies , both members of the 2019 Rugby World Cup winning squad, have also been banned for doping offences.

Three-cap prop Asenathi Ntlabakanye is the latest international to fall foul of the authorities, with the 27-year-old getting an 18-month suspension in May.

Incidents of doping on the country's highly competitive schoolboy circuit are also common.

While Dyanti, Jantjies and Ntlabakanye's positive tests were picked up by Saids, many of the Springbok squad play their club rugby overseas and will be subject to anti-doping tests there.

World Rugby's anti-doping programme, which includes biological markers and DNA as well as urine and blood analysis, stores samples after immediate testing to allow for further investigation as new techniques and technology are developed.

South Africa play France in the Nations Championship final on Sunday evening in the last match of their Test season.

articles.title: Ireland vs Australia: Andy Farrell using last Nations Championship match as World Cup preparation
articles.summary: Ireland aim to round out a successful November with victory over Australia in what Andy Farrell is treating as a dry-run before next year's World Cup.
articles.body:
Discussion about how Ireland head coach Andy Farrell would approach Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off against Australia was ended emphatically by the team announcement on Wednesday.

While Farrell would have been excused for fielding a rotated side in the wake of last week's bruising victory over world champions South Africa , he instead opted for continuity and is challenging his first-choice line-up to produce another chest-thumping 80-minute display against the Wallabies.

Farrell has made two changes from the side that started Saturday's 20-17 success over the Springboks in Dublin, both of which are enforced.

Jacob Stockdale replaces the ill Mack Hansen on the left wing while in-form back row Nick Timoney is restored at number eight in place of the banned Dan Sheehan.

While Ireland cannot win the inaugural Nations Championship, Farrell has emphasised the importance of Friday in the context of the team's journey to next year's World Cup.

Victory over Australia - who they beat 33-31 in Sydney in July - would be four wins in as many weekends. Do that down under next year and Ireland will find themselves in another World Cup quarter-final.

The six-day turnaround between last week's win over South Africa and Friday's contest with Australia serves as useful preparation for next year's tournament, where Ireland will have six days between their pool games against Portugal and Scotland and potentially a quarter and semi-final, should they reach that stage.

With no six-day turnarounds in the 2027 Six Nations, Farrell is keen to test his side within those parameters before they return to their provinces for a busy festive schedule.

While the World Cup unavoidably edges into view, Ireland's immediate priority is to close out a largely positive 2026 on a winning note.

Sobering defeats by France and New Zealand cast doubts over the squad's trajectory, but last week's narrow win over South Africa served as a reminder that Farrell's side can still mix it with the world's best.

And while slaying the Springboks may have restored hope among fans, senior squad figures have carefully tempered expectations as they attempt to round out the year with a 10th win from 12 Tests.

"If you're winning games by the skin of your teeth and not performing well you don't really gain that belief, but when you're playing well and then start winning well the belief comes and that's something that we certainly gained before the 2023 World Cup," said Tadhg Beirne, who will captain Ireland against Australia in Sheehan's absence.

"But we're building that and we're often talking about that in terms of creating that belief, creating that identity that we want to see of ourselves, but again we're nowhere near where we need to be if we want to be competing to win a World Cup next year.

"I think there's so much more growth but we have to keep delivering in these big games for everyone to feel it and I know how it feels back in 2023 going into that World Cup.

"I think everyone in that squad felt it and I think we're certainly on the way there and if we can keep performing the way we've been performing but getting better we'll certainly be there by next year."

Friday night is a big opportunity for Stockdale, who was not involved in the wins over Argentina, Fiji and South Africa.

Nearly nine years removed from his star-making performances for Joe Schmidt's Ireland in the 2018 Grand Slam campaign, the 30-year-old Ulster wing is no longer a nailed-on starter.

But having been picked ahead of Tommy O'Brien - who scored two tries in the win over Fiji - Stockdale must seize an opportunity to impress on what will be his first run-out at Twickenham since a try-scoring cameo off the bench in a behind-closed-doors Autumn Nations Cup defeat by England in November 2020.

Stockdale needn't look far for inspiration. Seven of his Ulster team-mates are in the matchday 23. Two of them - Stuart McCloskey and Timoney - have featured in all 12 Tests this year (alongside Beirne), while jet-heeled right winger Robert Baloucoune is enjoying his best run as an international after a couple of tries against South Africa last week.

In January 2016, Stockdale made his Ulster debut under the province's then director of rugby Les Kiss, the man now leading the Wallabies.

The 61-year-old replaced Schmidt following the July leg of the Nations Championship, and while scrutiny on the Queenslander intensified following defeats by England and Scotland, last week's 29-26 victory over Wales has boosted the Wallaby morale as they attempt to snap a six-game losing streak against the Irish.

Kiss, who was Ireland's defence coach during the historic 2009 Grand Slam triumph, has turned heads with his own selection in the number 11 jersey, with former Northampton Saints winger James Ramm earning his Test debut at the age of 28.

Kurtley Beale - who started Australia's last victory over Ireland in June 2018 - is an eye-catching addition to the bench as the 37-year-old closes in on a first Test cap in five years.

With Kalani Thomas earning a first start at scrum-half and a new back-row combination in Tom Hooper, Carlo Tizzano and Rob Valetini, it is an intriguing Wallabies line-up.

But if Ireland can replicate the intensity and edge they showed against South Africa, they may pass Farrell's World Cup rehearsal and ensure they approach the tantalising possibilities of 2027 in buoyant form.
